description: A browser-based, offline-first 3D physics engine that visualizes 8,151 exoplanets from NASA's TESS catalog. Built from scratch with Three.js and custom GLSL shaders, it models planetary transits, gravitational lensing, tidal deformation, auroras, and general relativistic black holes. No APIs, no servers—just the universe in your browser.
summary:
I developed the SPHEREx Sky Viewer & Exoplanet Atlas, a full-stack astrophysics suite that turns raw SPHEREx data into an interactive search for moving objects.

What I developed: The Sky Viewer features a custom all-sky map that queries the Caltech/IPCA IRSA archive via SIA2/TAP protocols. It downloads real FITS images, aligns them using WCS coordinates, and subtracts the median background to remove fixed stars. Users can then "blink" through the frames to spot moving objects—exoplanets, brown dwarfs, and asteroids. A "Visualize 3D System" button launches the Exoplanet Atlas, a WebGL engine built from scratch with custom GLSL shaders that renders 8,151 TESS planets, procedural atmospheres, tidal deformation, and a general relativistic black hole.

How it addresses the challenge: It provides the exact tool needed to find moving objects in the SPHEREx archive—the core goal of the "Planet X" challenge—while also giving users a 3D way to visualize their findings.

Why it is important: NASA generates petabytes of data, but the public cannot easily visualize it. This tool makes the search for distant worlds intuitive, interactive, and accessible to everyone. It bridges the gap between raw spectral data and a visual universe, empowering both researchers and the public to explore the cosmos.
details:
What it does:
The SPHEREx Sky Viewer & Exoplanet Atlas is a full-stack astrophysics suite. The Sky Viewer lets you search the entire sky (via an interactive map or coordinates) to find moving objects—exoplanets, brown dwarfs, and asteroids—in the SPHEREx archive. The Exoplanet Atlas is a 3D engine that visualizes 8,151 TESS planets, their atmospheres, and even a general relativistic black hole.

How it works:
The Sky Viewer queries the Caltech/IPAC IRSA archive (SIA2/TAP protocols), downloads real FITS images, aligns them using WCS coordinates, and subtracts the median background to remove fixed stars. Users "blink" through the frames to spot moving objects. The Atlas renders these planets in 3D using custom GLSL shaders for procedural atmospheres, tidal deformation, and gravitational lensing.

Benefits and Impact:
NASA generates petabytes of data, but the public can't easily visualize it. This tool makes the search for distant worlds intuitive and interactive. It turns raw spectral data into a visual universe, making astronomy accessible to everyone.

Tools Used:

  • Frontend: Vanilla HTML, CSS, JavaScript.
  • 3D Engine: Three.js with custom GLSL shaders.
  • Backend: Python 3 (standard library) for the CORS proxy and async TAP queries.
  • Data: Caltech/IPAC IRSA, NASA Exoplanet Archive, TESS catalog, DESI Legacy Surveys.

Creativity:
The integration is the creative part. Most tools show either 2D graphs or 3D models. This tool connects the raw data pipeline (custom FITS parsing, WCS alignment) to a 3D visualization engine. The custom FITS binary parser in JavaScript is rarely done in browser-based tools.

Factors Considered:

  • CORS Restrictions: Built a Python proxy with a manual CSV fallback.
  • Offline Capability: The Atlas runs entirely offline, ensuring a reliable demo.
  • Scalability: Designed to handle the full 8,151 TESS catalog and extend to the entire SPHEREx dataset.
